chapter.title: The model only talks. The agent does things.

cards.body:
A chatbot and an agent can run on the exact same brain, but only one of them can book you a flight.

Think of a new intern. Ask them a question and they answer, then sit back down. That's a chatbot. Give them a goal and the company card, and they keep getting up to do the next thing until the job is done. **That's an agent.**
cards.simpler: A chatbot and an agent can run on the same brain, but only one of them can book you a flight. Think of a new intern. Ask them a question and they answer, then sit back down. That's a chatbot. Give them a goal and the company card, and they keep getting up to do the next thing until the job is done. **That's an agent.**

cards.prompt: Same intern, three requests. Which one turns them into an agent?

options.text: "What's usually the cheapest day to fly to Lisbon?"
"Get me to Lisbon on Friday for under €200 and send me the booking."
"Write me a short poem about Lisbon."

whyNot.a: That's a question, not a goal: they answer once and stop, however useful the answer is.
whyNot.c: That's still one reply, however creative it is: nothing outside the chat changes.

cards.reteach: The test is whether the work ends at the reply. A chatbot gives one answer and waits for you. An agent takes a goal and keeps doing steps, like searching, comparing and paying, until the goal is met.

cards.title: Words in, words out
cards.body:
The brain inside ChatGPT is a *model*, a program that reads text and writes back text that's likely to come next, a few words at a time. That's its whole skill.

Picture the intern at an empty desk: no phone, no laptop, no company card. Ask anything and you'll get a smart answer, but nothing in the building moves.

A *chatbot* is that intern having one exchange with you. You ask, it replies, and **then it stops and waits for you**. Whatever needs doing next, you do it.
cards.simpler: The brain inside ChatGPT is called a model. It is a program that reads words and writes back words that are likely to come next. That is all it can do. Picture the intern at an empty desk with no phone, no laptop and no company card. They give smart answers, but nothing actually happens. A chatbot is that intern answering you once. **Then it stops and waits for you**, and any next step is yours to do.

cards.title: Same request, two answers
cards.body:
Sam asks a chatbot for the cheapest Friday flight to Lisbon. Back comes a tidy paragraph about budget airlines and early departures, and Sam still has no ticket.

Then Sam gives an agent the same request, plus permission to search, read the calendar and pay. It finds a €164 seat at 06:10, spots a dentist appointment at 08:30, books the €189 flight at 14:40 instead, and emails the receipt. **Same brain both times, but only one of them spent Sam's money.**
cards.simpler: Sam asks a chatbot for the cheapest Friday flight to Lisbon. Sam gets a neat paragraph about budget airlines and early flights, but still no ticket. Next, Sam asks an agent the same thing and lets it search, check the calendar and pay. It finds a €164 seat at 06:10, sees a dentist visit at 08:30, books the €189 flight at 14:40 instead, and emails the receipt. **Same brain both times, but only one spent Sam's money.**

cards.prompt: Tom has 2,000 emails and a spam problem. Which setup is an agent?

options.text: Tom pastes 20 emails into ChatGPT and asks which ones look like spam.
Tom gives an AI access to the inbox and the goal "move all spam to the bin", and it reads, decides and moves emails until it's done.
Tom asks ChatGPT for a list of signs that an email is spam.

whyNot.a: That's a chatbot giving a smart one-off answer: Tom still has to move every email himself.
whyNot.c: That's advice, not action: a list of tips never touches the inbox.

cards.reteach: Look for two things: can it touch something outside the chat, and does it keep going on its own? If you still have to do the clicking afterwards, it was a chatbot.

cards.title: Hands, and a reason to keep going
cards.body:
An *agent* is the same model with two extras. The first is *tools*, named actions it's allowed to ask for, like "search flights" or "send email". The second is a *loop*: each result comes back to the model so it can pick the next step.

You'd think the upgrade is a smarter brain. It isn't. It's a desk with a phone on it.

That's also the catch. A chatbot's worst slip is a wrong sentence you can ignore. An agent's worst slip is a paid ticket. **The risk moves from what it says to what it does.**
cards.simpler: An agent is the same model plus two extras: tools, actions it may ask for like "search flights", and a loop that hands each result back so it can pick the next step. The upgrade is not a smarter brain, just a phone on the desk. A chatbot's worst slip is a wrong sentence. An agent's is a paid ticket. **The risk moves from saying to doing.**

cards.body: Maya types "cancel my gym membership" into a chatbot and gets back a cheerful "Done! Here's your cancellation letter." Maya closes the tab, happy. Three months later the gym is still taking €40 a month, because nothing ever sent the letter. **To spot this, ask which tool it used.** If the answer is none, it only talked.
cards.simpler: Maya types "cancel my gym membership" into a chatbot. It replies, "Done! Here's your cancellation letter." Maya closes the tab, happy. Three months later the gym is still taking €40 a month, because nothing ever sent the letter. **To catch this, ask which tool it used.** If the answer is none, it only talked.

cards.prompt: Two apps run on the exact same AI model. App A answers questions. App B can read your calendar and send meeting invites. What makes B the agent?

options.text: B must be running on a smarter model.
B can take real actions and keeps going, step by step, toward a goal.
B gives longer, more detailed answers.

whyNot.a: That's the brain, not the job: the question says both apps share the same model.
whyNot.c: That's more talking, not doing: a long answer still changes nothing outside the chat.

cards.reteach: Swap the brain and nothing changes. Add hands and a loop and everything does. An agent is defined by what it can do, and by the fact that it keeps going, not by how clever it sounds.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A chatbot and an agent can use the same AI brain: the chatbot answers and stops, while the agent takes a goal and keeps acting until it's done. That's what makes agents useful, and it's also why their mistakes cost real money instead of just producing a wrong sentence.
cards.simpler: A chatbot and an agent can share the same AI brain. The chatbot answers and stops. The agent takes a goal and **keeps acting until the job is done**. That is what makes agents useful. It is also why their mistakes can cost real money, not just give you a wrong sentence.

cards.body:
Open ChatGPT or Claude and ask it to email a friend for you. Unless you've connected it to your email, it will write the message and hand it back. That's the gap between talking and doing.

Tomorrow: how one sentence, "book me a table", turns into eleven steps.
cards.simpler: Open ChatGPT or Claude and ask it to email a friend for you. Unless you have linked it to your email, it will write the message and hand it back to you to send. **That is the gap between talking and doing.** Tomorrow: how one sentence, "book me a table", turns into eleven steps.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain in 2 sentences why asking ChatGPT a question isn't an agent, but booking a flight with it would be.

dubious_claims: The hook and the 'Same brain, only one of them can book you a flight' framing imply ChatGPT itself can't act. ChatGPT has had an agent mode since 2025 that can browse sites and complete bookings, so the line 'only one of them can book you a flight' is misleading as written about ChatGPT.
'writes back the most likely next text' is an oversimplification: models usually sample from likely next words rather than always picking the single most likely one.
repairedFrom.why: The 'Hands, and a reason to keep going' card is about 121 words, and a textbook citation stalls it right before its best lines (the desk with a phone, the paid ticket).
repairedFrom.fix: Cut the Russell and Norvig sentence (about 24 words) so the desk-with-a-phone payoff comes sooner and the card drops under 100 words. Separately, move 'Tomorrow: how one sentence, "book me a table", turns into eleven steps.' from card 9 to the end of the try card so the chapter actually ends on the open loop.
